title: Differential syntactic and semantic encoding in LLMs
claim: Subtracting a structure-specific centroid sharply reduces similarity between matched items beyond a random ablation, showing the property is partly linearly encoded across depth.
layout: 2 side-by-side line plots, shared axes, legend inside left panel, shaded error bands
description: Two side-by-side line plots with a shared y-axis (Similarity, 0 to 1) and x-axis (relative depth, 0 to 1). Panel a) is titled Concatenation and panel b) is titled Average. Each panel has three curves with circular markers and thin shaded bands for one standard deviation. A blue curve (syntax twins) sits highest, at about 0.7 to 0.85 in a) and 0.4 to 0.7 in b). A red curve (random-ablated syntax twins) sits in the middle. A green curve (syntax-ablated syntax twins) sits lowest. In a), the red and green curves converge near 0.4 after about 0.4 depth. In b), the three curves stay separated. A legend sits in the lower left of panel a). The grid is light gray. The eye goes first to the blue curve and the gaps between the curves.
caption: Syntax similarity and its ablation. Similarity between equal-syntax sentences (syntax twins), such as those presented in Table [ref]. Panels a) and b) represent sentences by token concatenation and average, respectively. The shaded colored areas represent 1 standard deviation, calculated by subsampling five times half of the samples.
abstract: We study how syntactic and semantic information is encoded in inner layer representations of Large Language Models (LLMs), focusing on the very large DeepSeek-V3. We find that, by averaging hidden-representation vectors of sentences sharing syntactic structure or meaning, we obtain vectors that capture a significant proportion of the syntactic and semantic information contained in the representations. In particular, subtracting these syntactic and semantic ``centroids'' from sentence vectors strongly affects their similarity with syntactically and semantically matched sentences, respectively, suggesting that syntax and semantics are, at least partially, linearly encoded. We also find that the cross-layer encoding profiles of syntax and semantics are different, and that the two signals can to some extent be decoupled, suggesting differential encoding of these two types of linguistic information in LLM representations.
